definitions.definition: An event occurring in a network with implications for the security of a computer or the network; source may be internal or external
Preventing an unauthorised third party from accessing data exchanged between two endpoints
Detecting any unauthorised modification of transmitted data, ensured by digest algorithms and digital signatures
Guaranteeing that a resource can be accessed at the appropriate time; threatened by DoS/DDoS attacks
The sender of a message cannot deny having sent it; enforced by digital certificates issued by a Certification Authority (CA)
Verifying that someone is who they claim to be (e.g. password check, Kerberos, RADIUS)
Determining what an authenticated user is allowed to do (roles, permissions)
Mandatory Access Control – end-users cannot modify or transfer control over resources
Discretionary Access Control – the resource owner may grant rights to other users
Role-Based Access Control – permissions are assigned to a role within an organisation, then the role is assigned to a user
Rule-Based Access Control – access is assigned dynamically to a user based on a set of rules
A weakness in hardware or software that allows unauthorised users to gain access; no system is 100% secure
Denial of Service – attack that degrades or disables a service by overwhelming the server or network
Distributed DoS – DoS attack launched from many compromised hosts (agents) coordinated by handlers
Exploitation of programs that allocate insufficient buffer space, allowing execution of arbitrary commands with elevated privileges
Falsifying the source IP address in packets to hide the attacker's identity or bypass filters
Manipulating users through phishing, intimidation, impersonation, or flattery to obtain credentials or sensitive information
A social-engineering technique that impersonates a trusted entity to steal identity or credentials
Network or host-level system that controls traffic based on rules; deployed at the network layer
IP Security – suite of protocols (RFC 2401-2408) providing access control, data integrity, authentication, and confidentiality at the network layer
Transport Layer Security / Secure Sockets Layer – cryptographic protocols securing TCP connections; TLS 1.3 defined in RFC 8446
Secure Shell – protocol that negotiates an encrypted connection between a server and client with various authentication methods
Pretty Good Privacy – provides confidentiality and authentication for email and files using a suite of encryption algorithms (RFC 3156)
Public Key Infrastructure – system of services that issues, manages, and verifies digital certificates through Certification Authorities (CA) and Registration Authorities (RA)
Network Security Monitoring – collection, analysis, and assessment of indicators and alerts for detecting and responding to security incidents
Demilitarised Zone – network segment that separates sensitive internal data from publicly accessible servers
A specially configured decoy machine used to observe attacker behaviour; multiple honeypots form a honeynet
Risk analysis model: Damage potential, Reproducibility, Exploitability, Affected users, Discoverability
Threat model: Spoofing identity, Tampering with data, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege
Process of catching attackers after a security incident by analysing hardware (disks, RAM) and system logs

learning_objectives: Explain the CIA security triad and non-repudiation
Describe access control models (MAC, DAC, RoBAC, RuBAC) and their implementations
Identify people, hardware, protocol, and Internet-access vulnerability categories
Classify attacks by profile (opportunistic/intermediate/sophisticated) and mode (DoS, buffer overflow, sniffing, social engineering, malware, etc.)
Explain prevention principles across all OSI/TCP-IP layers
Describe survival properties: resistance, recognition, and adaptation
Outline the NSM process: detection, identification, validation, and reaction
Apply risk-analysis methodologies (DREAD, STRIDE, OCTAVE, OSSTMM) and the SANS incident-response framework
Describe security protocols: IPSec, TLS/SSL, SSH, PGP, S/MIME
Identify wireless-specific threats and countermeasures (WEP, WPA, WTLS)
